summary: MPLS LSP ping and traceroute test ECMP paths, with ping checking connectivity and traceroute isolating faults, as described in RFC 4379. This proposed standard describes how to run them on LSPs that use entropy labels for load balancing.

eli5.summary: Roads that split traffic by label need testing along each branch. This explains how to run the checking tools when routers choose branches by a special label.

questions: what is an entropy label in mpls
how does mpls traceroute work with ecmp
what are the l and e flags in lsp ping
subtitle: Extending MPLS ping and traceroute so they can still exercise every load-balanced path when entropy labels are in use.

tldr.problem: When an LSP uses an entropy label, LSP ping and traceroute lose the ability to discover and exercise Equal-Cost Multipath (ECMP) paths if routers along the path balance load in different ways, for example by label at some hops and by IP header at others.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds an Entropy Label FEC sub-TLV, two new DS flags (L and E) that a responder uses to say how it balances load and whether it pushes ELI/EL, and Multipath Information Type 10, which carries IP addresses, labels and associated labels together.
tldr.outcome: Initiators and responders follow defined procedures to keep tracing ECMP paths across mixed networks. Only a subset of load-balancing designs is supported. The RFC updates RFC 6790.

today: RFC 8012 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2016. It updates RFC 6790 and, according to the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated by a later RFC.

sections.title: The Problem with Entropy Labels
sections.content:
MPLS LSP ping and traceroute (RFC 4379) test ECMP paths. In traceroute, the initiating LSR sends echo requests with TTL 1, 2, 3 and so on, and learns Multipath Information from each transit LSR. That information carries either IP addresses (types 2, 4 and 8) or labels (type 9) in the DDMAP TLV, so the initiator can steer later probes down a chosen path.

Once an LSP uses an entropy label (RFC 6790), this breaks in several cases. The initiator may send IP information to a router that balances on labels, or label information to a router that balances on IP. A router that pushes an entropy label indicator and entropy label (ELI/EL) must also return the EL that goes with each IP address or label, otherwise the initiator cannot keep exercising specific paths downstream.

The RFC notes these scenarios are common, because real deployments mix nodes that support ELI/EL with nodes that do not. To use the method end to end, all LSRs on the LSP must understand the new flags and the new Multipath type.
sections.eli5: Some routers pick lanes by looking at the address and some by looking at the special number. The checker needs to speak the right language to each one, and the old checker only knew one language.

sections.title: Load-Balancer Types
sections.content:
The RFC names roles in the exchange. The initiating LSR sends an MPLS echo request. The responder LSR receives it and sends an echo reply.

It also classifies LSRs by what they hash on. An IP-based load balancer uses fields from the IP header and ignores any flow or entropy label. A label-based load balancer uses an entropy label from the stack and ignores IP header fields. A label and IP-based balancer uses both. These terms describe how a received echo request is handled by the responder.
sections.eli5: There are three kinds of lane-pickers: ones that read the address, ones that read the special number, and ones that read both.

sections.title: The Entropy Label FEC
sections.content:
The ELI is a reserved label with the value 7 and no explicit FEC, so it is accounted for with the Nil FEC in the Target FEC Stack TLV. The EL itself is a label with a discretionary value, not from the reserved range. So the RFC defines a new EL FEC sub-TLV, sub-type 33, so that the Target FEC Stack can describe the EL clearly, including in cases such as a flow-aware pseudowire where no ELI is present.

The sub-TLV has length 4. It holds a 20-bit Label value, which is the actual label inserted in the stack, followed by an MBZ field that MUST be zero when sent and ignored on receipt.
sections.eli5: The special number gets its own entry on the checker's list so that everyone knows exactly which number is meant.

sections.title: DS Flags L and E, and Multipath Type 10
sections.content:
Two new flags are added to the DS Flags field of the DDMAP TLV. Both MUST NOT be set in echo requests and SHOULD be ignored when received. L (label-based load balance indicator) is set by an LSR that balances on a label and not set by one that balances on IP. E (ELI/EL push indicator) is set by an LSR that pushes ELI/EL. Together they give four combinations, such as L=0, E=1 for an LSR that balances on IP and pushes ELI/EL.

The new Multipath Information Type 10 (IP and label set) has three sections: an IP address set, a label set, and an associated label set. The type byte of the first two sections is 0 when the section is omitted, and a section that is omitted has its length set to zero. The associated labels MUST be omitted in an echo request. A midpoint that pushes ELI/EL SHOULD include them in its reply, and each one maps by position to an IP address or label in the other sections. For example, three IP addresses need three associated labels.
sections.eli5: Each router raises two little flags in its answer: one says how it picks lanes, the other says whether it adds a special number. The new answer format lists which number goes with which lane.

sections.title: Initiator and Responder Procedures
sections.content:
The initiating LSR keeps a boolean called EL_LSP. It is true when the initiator pushes ELI/EL, and also set true when it receives a reply with L=0, E=1. When EL_LSP is true and the initiator sends non-zero Multipath Information, it MUST use type 10 unless the responder cannot handle it, and it MUST include both IP and label multipath information and omit the associated labels. In other cases it MAY use types 2, 4, 8, 9 or 10. If a reply is empty or inconsistent with its flags, the initiator MAY continue on a best-effort basis.

A responder first decides whether the initiator supports this extension: it SHOULD conclude so if the request contains type 10 or an EL FEC in the Target FEC Stack. If not, it MUST clear both new flags and MUST NOT use type 10. A type 10 request that lacks IP Multipath Information or includes associated labels is malformed and gets return code 1 ("Malformed echo request received").

Four sub-procedures cover the responder's load-balancing technique: IP-based without ELI/EL push, IP-based with push, label-based without push, and label-based with push. Each sets the flags to match, replies with type 0 when it is sent an unusable type, and, for pushing LSRs, fills the associated label list. A flow-aware MS-PW stitching LSR behaves like the no-push label-based case if it carries over the same flow label, and like the pushing case if it replaces the flow label.
sections.eli5: The checker keeps a note saying 'this road uses special numbers' and then asks the right question. Each router answers in the way that matches how it picks lanes.

sections.title: Supported and Unsupported Cases
sections.content:
The RFC acknowledges many possible load-balancer designs: IP-based, label-based, or both, hashing the entire label stack, the top N labels, or the bottom N labels, plus differing handling of multiple entropy labels and reserved labels. Supporting all of them would need fairly complex OAM procedures with little benefit if most implementations use a small subset.

It therefore supports cases where the balancer is IP-based, or label-based over the entire label stack with only the first (top-most) entropy label counted when several are present. It cites RFC 6790 and RFC 7325 as reasons to expect this. Other cases are out of scope.
sections.eli5: There are too many ways to pick lanes to test them all, so the RFC picks the most common ways and works well for those.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
LSP ping and traceroute already allow ECMP discovery. This document makes that more precise when ELI/EL is used. The RFC notes that sourcing or inspecting LSP ping packets can be used for network reconnaissance.

The extension needs minor extra processing: responders that push ELI/EL compute and return multipath data including the associated EL, and initiators store both IP and label information. The Denial-of-Service considerations of RFC 4379, which regulate LSP ping traffic going to the control plane, already apply, as do the security measures in RFC 6424 and RFC 6790.
sections.eli5: Someone could use the checker to learn how the network is laid out, so the usual limits on the checker still apply.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: IANA assigned three values in the MPLS LSP Ping Parameters registry: sub-TLV type 33 for the Entropy label FEC, DS Flags bit 5 for E (ELI/EL push indicator) and bit 4 for L (label-based load balance indicator), and Multipath Type 10 for IP and label set.
sections.eli5: The official list of numbers got three new entries for the new pieces.
